newsitem.title: UK: FORECAST - UK retail prices to soften on stg rise.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - UK retail prices to soften on stg rise.

text.p: British retail prices are likely to have softened in April, helped by the effects of a stronger pound feeding into lower import prices, analysts said.
The Reuters consensus forecast for April data due on Thursday is for retail prices excluding mortgage interest payments (RPIX) to show a 2.6 percent rise year-on-year, down from 2.7 percent in March.
Headline RPI is forecast at 0.6 percent month-on-month and 2.5 percent year-on-year.
"Its all coming through on the goods side, its all due to sterling," said Ciaran Barr, UK economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.
Sterling has rocketed since last August but analysts disagreed about the extent of its effect.

"It can be up to a year before big movements in the output prices actually show up in the RPI," said Jonathan Loynes, UK economist at HSBC Markets. "The lag can be variable, there's no certainty about it."
Loynes and other analysts agreed sterling strength would certainly have fed into some core import goods.
"We should also see the benefit of lower oil prices," said Barr. "Sterling has a massive impact on food prices because we import so much food."
But other analysts said food could actually push retail prices higher rather than reinforcing the downtrend prompted by the strong pound.
"The main risk to this forecast lies with the drier-than-usual and warmer-than-usual April weather, which may have affected food prices," Lehman Brothers said in a client note.

A softening of the RPIX figure to 2.6 percent would take inflation closer to the target of 2.5 percent set by the last Conservative government and likely to be formally confirmed by the new Labour administration.
But analysts said the outlook was for inflationary pressures to build as the service sector gathered steam, a view echoed by the Bank of England in its quarterly Inflation Report on Tuesday.
"You've got to see it as a temporary fall," said Barr. "We are going to see strong inflationary pressures coming through at the end of this year."
The central bank said in its Inflation Report that on present evidence, "there is still likely to be a need for some further moderate tightening of policy in the months ahead."
Michael Saunders of Salomon Brothers said April RPI was exceptionally hard to forecast because it included a range of annual changes to items such as rents, water charges and council tax.
Housing depreciation costs had been surprisingly weak in the past couple of months and could rebound, he wrote in a client note.

"On balance we expect these effects, plus the downward effect on prices from sterling's rise, to result in stable figures for headline and underlying inflation in April, but there could easily be a surprise figure on either the upside or downside," Saunders said.

Lehman Brothers said changes in indirect taxation at the start of the year, with council tax rising around 6.6 percent on average and water charges up by about 4.0 percent, were unlikely to have had a great impact on the RPI data.
"These are unlikely to be any greater than the changes seen last year so there is no upward pressure on the inflation rate from these sources," it said.
